marker_malcolm.persona: Malcolm Ryan, COMP3180 convenor, reading the thirty-eighth of forty proposals and judging whether this one convinces me it is interesting, that the student will learn something, that the tools are a valid choice, that the pieces fit, and that it talks to the state of the art.

criteria.descriptor_quote: At least five distinct and high-quality sources with a common theme relating to the project topic. Sources are very well summarised and evaluated in terms of their relevance, lessons for and usefulness to the outlined project. Review synthesises and abstracts key patterns and relationships from the literature to motivate the project.
criteria.why_not_higher: The source count and quality clear the HD line on paper (six peer-reviewed venues, common theme) and every entry avoids my pet peeve: each names a method, a number and a limitation, then says what is taken. That is genuinely strong. What keeps it out of 'expertly synthesises' is that the argument the review exists to make is conceded rather than built. Not one of the six studies observed a producer, and the whole transfer rests on two sentences at the very end: 'None of these studies observed a game producer; I take their mechanisms and test the transfer.' That is the load-bearing claim of the section and it arrives as a closing admission in a paragraph of forty-eight words. Second, the one place the review applies a source to the design is the place it is weakest: 'I take it as a design constraint: every report is addressed to the producer, removing this mechanism.' Stray's finding is that a stand-up written for the manager degrades into status reporting the team tunes out; a report written for the producer is the manager-facing case, so the mechanism is accepted, not removed. I can knock that over in one question. Third, the Bertram quotation, 'often bugs that are that critical don't even get filed because by the time that you would go to file it, the bug is already resolved', is about work too fast to file, while the Introduction's motivating case is a two-day refactor too large to fit a ticket. Vivid quote, adjacent claim. Finally the density: the opening paragraph asks the reader to hold six author names and two different taxonomies at once, and I read this section twice before the three-mechanism structure came clear. A review I have to read twice is not an expert one.
criteria.single_change_to_next_band: Promote the transfer argument from the closing concession to the spine. Rewrite the final paragraph so it states plainly what the six studies collectively establish about any reader of a work record, then says why a game producer is the hardest case of that reader (no code, most of the week non-code per Pascarella), and only then names the three competing mechanisms and which one the study will discriminate. Pay for it by cutting the Stray paragraph's method preamble ('built a grounded theory of the daily stand-up from 12 teams in consulting, telecoms and software companies, none of them game teams' to 'studied daily stand-ups in twelve non-game teams') and the Washburn trailing clause.

criteria.descriptor_quote: Outlines a sensible plan with clear and specific learning goals for developing industry-relevant skills. Identifies a considered research question with an appropriate and achievable mixed methodology for evaluation. Overview of scoping work undertaken provides a strongly convincing argument for the feasibility of the project. Includes a description of specific and measurable project deliverables clearly demonstrating these goals and satisfying unit requirements.
criteria.why_not_higher: The scoping is the best thing in this document and is HD on its own: a Unity Editor package docked and loaded on real data (Figure 2), six repositories measured, nine weeks of naming presence, a build-report probe, and — the part I actually credit — scoping that changed the design, since 'No public Unity repository I screened links issues densely enough' killed the tracker arm rather than being quietly ignored. The tiers are exactly the Kickstarter structure I asked for, with a named overrun order. So why not HD overall: the methodology is misallocated against the question. The headline question is answered by the weakest instrument in the study — 'I report percentage agreement and, per reader, Cohen's kappa against my marking; over ten items these are indicative, not inferential' — which makes the author the gold standard for the very question the project exists to answer, and computes a statistic over ten items with a participant floor of five. Meanwhile the properly designed arm, the counterbalanced treatment-versus-baseline comprehension test with an unanswerable catch item and per-week baselines, answers Sub-question 2. The strong method is on the small question. Compounding it, the reader is never shown the two sub-questions together: 'Sub-question 1 operationalises the main question' arrives as a label with no referent, and Sub-question 2 surfaces a paragraph later, so I had to reconstruct which arm answers what. On the goals: four, correctly framed as capabilities not deliverables, reaching Evaluate and Create — good. But 'Understand: diagnose why a team's production record under-reports its work' puts an Analyse verb under an Understand label, and the Create goal's measure ('I can tie each layout decision to a named reader need') tests justification, not creation. The ladder is claimed more cleanly than it is evidenced. Smaller: 'The committed tier (11 hours) delivers the extractor' budgets eleven hours for something Figure 2 shows already running, which is the first variance question I will ask at A3.
criteria.single_change_to_next_band: Make the strong arm serve the headline question. Reframe the ten-need classification as a descriptive map whose finding is the disagreements (drop kappa entirely), and state explicitly that the comprehension comparison is the study's test of the main question for one artefact — the asset layer — with the classification sheet establishing the boundary of what the other artefacts could reach. Then number both sub-questions in the Introduction so the reader sees the shape before the detail.

criteria.descriptor_quote: The report is easy to read and uses appropriate language and structure. It meets the word count, referencing and other submission requirements. It may contain a few minor spelling, grammatical or referencing errors.
criteria.why_not_higher: Mechanically this is close to spotless — APA is consistent with DOIs throughout, the body is 2,471 words plus a 26-word cover against a 2,500 limit excluding references, the template's sections are all present, and the three figures are relevant, captioned and called out in text (Figure 3's annotated prefab hunk is the clearest single thing in the document). I found no spelling or grammatical errors. What it is not is 'very easy to read'. Almost every sentence carries a claim, a number and a qualification simultaneously, and the methodology opens on a 62-word chain with four clauses and two parentheticals: 'The study is a within-subjects comparison: eight readers (COMP3151 producers, or teammates briefed into the role) each read two ChangeLens reports for different SS3D weeks, one naming the changed scenes and prefabs (the treatment) and one not (the baseline), counterbalanced by week and order; six of them then think aloud while drafting a two-minute stand-up update from the report alone.' The Introduction does the same thing the A1 presentation did: it fires the tool, the research question, the study shape and the competitive landscape inside roughly 200 words, so 'Two arms answer it' uses study jargon before a study has been mentioned, and 'None turns the Unity asset layer into a week's account for a producer' lands the novelty claim before the reader knows what the Unity asset layer is. Scoping Evidence then runs five unlabelled paragraphs — design, recruitment, quantitative arm, qualitative arm, fidelity check — with no signposting after the two bold leads. Timings are given as 'Each session runs 45 minutes: 5 to brief, 12 per report to read it and answer six items (Appendix B), 6 for the ten-need sheet and 10 for the think-aloud and follow-up (six readers)', with units dropped and the arithmetic left to me. This is a document that rewards a careful second reading, and I will not be giving it one. Torn between CR and D, I report CR: the images and referencing lift it above the CR anchor, but the readability clause of D is not met.
criteria.single_change_to_next_band: Break the four densest sentences into two or three each — the study-design opener, the session-timing list, the Introduction's last paragraph and the Sub-question 1 definition — and add two bold micro-heads inside Scoping Evidence ('Participants and recruitment', 'Measures'). All of it is word-neutral or word-negative; none of it needs new content. That alone is worth the band.

top_changes.location: Scoping Evidence (Study design) — "Sub-question 1 operationalises the main question. For each need surfaced by the tool study (Deliverable 1), which artefact could supply it, fully or partly: the tracker, the repository or the Unity asset layer?"
top_changes.problem: The two sub-questions are never stated together anywhere in the document. Sub-question 1 arrives as a numbered label with no prior referent; Sub-question 2 appears a paragraph later at the end of a long block. A marker checking 'is the methodology appropriate to the question' has to reconstruct the mapping from arm to question by hand, and the answer to that check is the largest single share of the Project Proposal criterion.
top_changes.fix: In the Introduction, replace "Two arms answer it. Eight readers sort ten common producer needs by which artefact could answer each. They also read two versions of the report: one names the changed scenes and prefabs (the Unity asset layer), one does not." (approx. 46 w) with: "Two sub-questions answer it. (1) For each need, which artefact could supply it: the tracker, the repository or the Unity asset layer? (2) Does naming the changed scenes and prefabs improve a reader's comprehension of the week?" (approx. 38 w). Then in Study design, cut the quoted sentences to: "Sub-question 1 runs over the needs surfaced by Deliverable 1; each is marked derivable, partly derivable or not." and cut "Sub-question 2 tests one artefact against one need: does naming the changed scenes and prefabs improve a reader's comprehension of the week?" to "Sub-question 2 is the report comparison described above." PAYS FOR ITSELF: net saving approx. 55 words across the two sections, no new content.
top_changes.mark_impact: Project Proposal +2 to +3 (methodology legibility is the clause it is losing on); Communication +2. The single highest-value edit available.

top_changes.location: Scoping Evidence (Study design) — "I report percentage agreement and, per reader, Cohen's kappa against my marking; over ten items these are indicative, not inferential."
top_changes.problem: Kappa computed against the author's own marking makes the author the gold standard for the exact question the project exists to answer, and over ten items with eight raters (floor five) the statistic is noise. Naming it 'indicative, not inferential' is honest but does not rescue it: a marker who knows methods reads a statistic that should not have been computed, and it sits on the headline research question.
top_changes.fix: Replace with: "I report, per need, how many readers agree with my marking and how many split. The split needs are the finding: they name what the artefacts cannot settle." (approx. 29 w vs approx. 24 w). PAY FOR IT by cutting the later sentence in the same paragraph, "Each disagreement is a finding about what the artefacts cannot say." (11 w), which the replacement now absorbs. Net saving approx. 6 words. Keep the intra-rater check in the qualitative arm ('a quarter is re-coded after a week') — that one is legitimate and should stay.
top_changes.mark_impact: Project Proposal +2. Removes the one methodological claim in the document I would attack first, and converts it into the evaluative move (naming what cannot be settled) that the criterion rewards.

top_changes.location: Scoping Evidence (Study design) — "The study is a within-subjects comparison: eight readers (COMP3151 producers, or teammates briefed into the role) each read two ChangeLens reports for different SS3D weeks, one naming the changed scenes and prefabs (the treatment) and one not (the baseline), counterbalanced by week and order; six of them then think aloud while drafting a two-minute stand-up update from the report alone."
top_changes.problem: 62 words, four clauses, two parentheticals and a semicolon, at the head of the methodology — the densest sentence in the document sitting at the point where the marker most needs to grasp the design quickly. This is the A1 failure mode (technical detail with no landing space) reproduced in prose.
top_changes.fix: Split into three, word-neutral: "The study is a within-subjects comparison. Eight readers — COMP3151 producers, or teammates briefed into the role — each read two ChangeLens reports for different SS3D weeks: one names the changed scenes and prefabs (treatment), one does not (baseline). Week and order are counterbalanced, and six readers then think aloud while drafting a two-minute stand-up update from the report alone." No cut required: the replacement is within two words of the original.
top_changes.mark_impact: Communication +2. Zero word cost, zero content change, and it is the sentence that most determines whether the reader grasps the study on the first pass.

top_changes.location: Introduction — "Seven existing tools each cover one part of this (Appendix A): they summarise tickets and commits for engineers, take manual entry from game teams, or show asset history to developers and artists. None turns the Unity asset layer into a week's account for a producer."
top_changes.problem: The novelty claim is the most technical sentence in the document's most context-setting section, and it depends on a term ('the Unity asset layer') the reader has not met and cannot yet picture. The A1 marker's exact words were 'You jumped straight into very technical details without providing context.' This is that, in the first 200 words, and it also crowds out the breathing room the Introduction needs.
top_changes.fix: Move it to the end of the Scoping Evidence 'Prototype and corpus' paragraph — after Figures 2 and 3 have shown the reader what the asset layer actually is — and compress to: "Seven existing tools each cover one part of this (Appendix A); none turns the Unity asset layer into a week's account for a producer." PAYS FOR ITSELF: net saving approx. 24 words, and the claim now sits beside the evidence that supports it rather than 1,500 words away from it.
top_changes.mark_impact: Communication +1 to +2; Project Proposal +1 (the originality claim reads as demonstrated rather than asserted). Frees approx. 24 words for change 1's Introduction rewrite.

top_changes.location: Literature Review (Stray paragraph) — "I take it as a design constraint: every report is addressed to the producer, removing this mechanism."
top_changes.problem: Logically backwards, and it is the one claim in the review I can knock over in a single Q&A question. Stray's finding is that a stand-up addressed to the manager rather than the team degrades into status reporting others tune out. ChangeLens writes for the producer — that is the manager-facing case. The design instantiates the mechanism; it does not remove it. Claiming otherwise turns the strongest analytical section of the proposal into an own goal.
top_changes.fix: Replace with: "I take it as a design constraint I cannot escape: the report is addressed to the producer, so this mechanism is accepted, not removed — which is why the tool must cost the team nothing to produce." (approx. 37 w vs 16 w). PAY FOR IT in the same paragraph: cut "built a grounded theory of the daily stand-up from 12 teams in consulting, telecoms and software companies, none of them game teams" to "studied daily stand-ups in twelve non-game teams (grounded theory)" (saves approx. 13 w) and cut "postmortems cannot settle the question, so I look in artefacts" to "so I look in artefacts" (saves approx. 7 w). Net saving approx. 1 word, and the rewrite now also states why passive extraction is the answer to Stray, tying the source to the design.
top_changes.mark_impact: Literature Review +1 to +2. Turns the weakest evaluative move in the review into one of its better ones, and pre-empts an obvious Q&A attack.

top_changes.location: Deliverables — "The committed tier (11 hours) delivers the extractor, both report versions and object naming (Figure 3)."
top_changes.problem: Figure 2 shows the extractor built, docked and loaded on real data. Budgeting eleven hours to 'deliver the extractor' invites exactly the question I will ask at A3 — you had it working in September, what were the eleven hours for? — and it makes the strongest piece of scoping evidence in the document look like it is being double-counted as future work.
top_changes.fix: Replace with: "The committed tier (11 hours) turns the working extractor (Figure 2) into the producer-facing page, builds both report versions, and adds object naming (Figure 3)." (approx. 25 w vs 15 w). PAY FOR IT in the same paragraph: cut "parses Unity's build report (already readable; Appendix C) and names failed steps and the three largest asset-size changes" to "parses Unity's build report (Appendix C) for failed steps and the three largest asset-size changes" (saves approx. 5 w), and "An overrun consumes the challenge tier first, then the stretch tier." to "An overrun drops the challenge tier, then the stretch tier." (saves approx. 4 w). Net cost approx. 1 word.
top_changes.mark_impact: Project Proposal +1. Protects the feasibility argument, which is currently the criterion's strongest clause, from reading as padded.

top_changes.location: Learning Goals — "**Understand:** diagnose why a team's production record under-reports its work" and "**Create:** ... *Measure:* given an unfamiliar Unity week, I can tie each layout decision to a named reader need, two defended against a rejected alternative."
top_changes.problem: The Bloom's ladder is claimed more cleanly than it is evidenced at both ends. 'Diagnose' is an Analyse verb sitting under an Understand label, and the Create goal's measure tests justification of design decisions — an Evaluate act — not creation. A marker checking the spread sees four levels named and two of them measured at the wrong rung. The middle goal also merges Apply and Analyse into one rung with an Analyse-only measure, so 'Apply' is asserted and never measured.
top_changes.fix: Understand: swap 'diagnose' for 'explain' (word-neutral) — the existing measure ('I can state each mechanism unaided, with its source and a breakdown it predicts') is already an Understand measure and then matches. Create: replace the measure with "*Measure:* a reader who has never opened SS3D can draft a stand-up update from the page unaided, with every layout decision tied to a named reader need." PAY FOR IT by cutting "two defended against a rejected alternative" (6 w), which duplicates the rejection move already measured in the Evaluate goal ('three needs where I name the artefact I rejected and why'). Net saving approx. 2 words.
top_changes.mark_impact: Project Proposal +1. Goals are otherwise the strongest part of the plan — the A1 marker singled them out ('Good learning goals') — so this is protecting an asset, not repairing a hole.

top_changes.location: Scoping Evidence (recruitment) — "proxies get a one-page scenario and stand in for studio producers, a limit I report."
top_changes.problem: There are two layers of proxy here, not one, and only the first is disclosed. Student readers stand in for studio producers, and SS3D — a repository none of them has ever worked on — stands in for the reader's own project. A real producer's advantage is that they know the team and the plan; a stranger to the codebase has none of that context, which should make any naming of scenes and prefabs help more than it would in the field. That biases the treatment effect upward, and the proposal does not say so. Naming the direction of a bias is the evaluative move the rubric asks for; 'a limit I report' is the move it does not.
top_changes.fix: Replace with: "proxies get a one-page scenario and stand in for studio producers; reading an unfamiliar project also strips the context a real producer has, which should favour the treatment, so I report the difference as an upper bound." (approx. 38 w vs 15 w). PAY FOR IT in the same paragraph: cut "I recruit at the Weeks 9 and 10 COMP3151 pracs and my COMP3180 prac" to "I recruit at the Weeks 9-10 COMP3151 and COMP3180 pracs" (saves approx. 5 w), "Participation is voluntary, with verbal consent and de-identified reporting." to "Participation is voluntary; consent is verbal and reporting de-identified." (saves approx. 2 w), and "The floor is five readers and five think-alouds." to "The floor is five of each." (saves approx. 4 w). Net cost approx. 12 words — cover the remainder from change 1's 55-word saving.
top_changes.mark_impact: Project Proposal +1 to +2. This is the difference between disclosing a limitation and reasoning about it, which is the Evaluate-level thinking the goals promise.

top_changes.location: Literature Review (Bertram paragraph) — "One participant said, \"often bugs that are that critical don't even get filed because by the time that you would go to file it, the bug is already resolved\" (P05, p. 296)."
top_changes.problem: The quotation is about work too fast to file. The Introduction's motivating case is 'A two-day refactor can leave no ticket' — work too large to fit a ticket. Both are real, but they are different failures, and the quotation is doing rhetorical work for a claim it does not actually support. On a careful read this is the one place in the review where the evidence and the argument are misaligned, and it is the first source the marker meets.
top_changes.fix: Shorten the quotation to its operative clause and add the bridge: "One participant described bugs 'already resolved' by the time anyone would file them (P05, p. 296). The same entry cost silences work at both ends: too fast to be worth filing, and too large to fit one ticket." (approx. 42 w vs approx. 38 w). PAY FOR IT in the same paragraph by cutting "Their remedy, a simplified filing interface (p. 297), still asks the under-reporting party to report, so I do not take it: my evaluation scores each report against the team's history, not its tickets." to "Their remedy, a simplified filing interface (p. 297), still asks the under-reporting party to report, so I score reports against the team's history, not its tickets." (saves approx. 7 w). Net saving approx. 3 words.
top_changes.mark_impact: Literature Review +1. Closes the only gap between a quoted source and the claim it is cited for.

top_changes.location: Scoping Evidence — "Each session runs 45 minutes: 5 to brief, 12 per report to read it and answer six items (Appendix B), 6 for the ten-need sheet and 10 for the think-aloud and follow-up (six readers)."
top_changes.problem: Units are dropped, the doubling of the 12 minutes is invisible, and the reader must compute 5 + 24 + 6 + 10 = 45 to check the claim. The trailing '(six readers)' dangles off the wrong noun. A feasibility number the marker cannot verify at a glance is a feasibility number that does no work.
top_changes.fix: Replace with: "Each session runs 45 minutes: 5 min briefing, 12 min per report for two reports (six items each, Appendix B), 6 min for the ten-need sheet, and 10 min of think-aloud for the six readers who do it." (approx. 40 w vs approx. 34 w). PAY FOR IT in the adjacent sentence: cut "A pilot runs first; its data are excluded." and "Week difficulty is a rival explanation, so per-week baseline scores are reported too." to "A pilot runs first, excluded from the data; week difficulty is a rival explanation, so per-week baseline scores are reported." (saves approx. 6 w). Net neutral.
top_changes.mark_impact: Communication +1. Small, but it is in the paragraph a marker uses to decide whether the 65 hours are real.

evidence_needed.item: Whether the rendered PDF is producing visibly loose justification. Text extraction from the PDF shows broken words ('Pascare lla', 'becom es', 'mecha nism', 'wha t', 'splas h') that do not exist in the markdown source, which is the signature of full justification stretching inter-letter spacing on narrow lines.
evidence_needed.what_would_settle_it: Open the PDF at 150% and eyeball pages 2-4. If words are visibly gappy, either switch the body to left-aligned or enable hyphenation in build-docx-v2.js and rebuild. This is a Communication-criterion risk that costs nothing to remove, and a marker reading on screen will see it.

evidence_needed.item: Whether the Unity Experiment Framework is defensible as 'the tracker-plus-repository case' when Appendix A records it at 20 genuine issue references per 100 commits against a stated threshold of 30. The body says 'No public Unity repository I screened links issues densely enough' and then uses the best of the failures, and Deliverable 1's success measure commits to checking 25 needs 'against the Unity Experiment Framework'.
evidence_needed.what_would_settle_it: Either one sentence stating that no repository met the threshold so the best-linked one is used as an illustrative, not representative, case; or a short re-screen of two or three further Unity repositories with dense issue linkage. The first costs about fifteen words and removes an internal contradiction a careful marker will find.

evidence_needed.item: Whether eight COMP3151 readers will actually sit 45-minute sessions in Weeks 11-12 while their own teams build toward a 3 November release. Recruitment is named as 'The biggest risk' and the mitigation is a floor of five.
evidence_needed.what_would_settle_it: Three named people with verbal commitments before 20 September, noted in the development diary. That converts the largest feasibility risk from a plan into evidence, and it is the kind of thing I will ask about in the prac.

evidence_needed.item: Whether Ko et al.'s 21 information types transfer to producers at all. Deliverable 1 seeds 25 needs from a taxonomy elicited entirely from developers, and the proposal already concedes that 'the debugging kinds are not' a producer's questions.
evidence_needed.what_would_settle_it: A rough count now of how many of the 21 plausibly survive the transfer. If it is fewer than about ten, the seeding needs a second source or an explicit statement that the taxonomy is a starting frame that the tool study is expected to break.

evidence_needed.item: Which of the six counted sources have been read in full, as the bracketed placeholder after the GenAI statement asks.
evidence_needed.what_would_settle_it: The exercise I set in the Week 4 lecture: write a potted summary of each source from memory, in your own words, before touching the draft again. If any one of the six cannot be summarised without opening it, that is the source to read this week. The review's per-source detail is good enough that this is very likely already true, but it is the one thing the document cannot evidence to me.

marker_malcolm.notes: Honest expectation for the real mark: 74-79, most likely 76-78. I would be surprised by anything above 82 and not shocked by 72. The band is D across the content criteria and CR on Communication, and the gap between what this document contains and what it communicates is the whole story. On substance this is one of the better proposals in the cohort: six peer-reviewed sources each summarised with a method, a number, a stated limitation and a named use; three competing mechanisms set up so the study can discriminate between them; a Unity Editor tool actually built and shown running on real data; a corpus screen whose negative result changed the design rather than being buried; nine deliverables with success measures and hours summing to 65 with 15 in prac; and committed/stretch/challenge tiers with a named overrun order. The gap is framed correctly for this unit — 'My gap is judging what a team's artefacts can and cannot tell a producer' is a gap in the student's own learning, which is what I asked for, not a claim to new knowledge for the world. On delivery it is exhausting. Nearly every sentence carries a claim, a number and a qualification at once, and I had to read the methodology twice to work out which arm answers which question. The A1 feedback on this student was 'So much information in each slide. Need to give a general overview first... It was hard to know what the presentation was about. Good learning goals.' Three of those four sentences still apply to this document, and I have weighted them accordingly — the goals are still good, and the density is still the thing standing between a D and an HD. Note that every one of my top ten changes is word-neutral or word-negative; the body is at 2,471 plus a 26-word cover against 2,500 excluding references, and nothing here needs more room, only better spacing of what is already there. Two minor items I did not spend a change on: Figure 1's caption cites a '12-57%' range that is not plotted in the figure (it is in Appendix A, so this is defensible, but a reader may look for it on the chart); and there is no table-of-contents field, which I am told is a known consequence of generating from markdown. The bracketed CONFIRM line after the GenAI statement is noted as a known placeholder and marked as if absent. The GenAI statement itself is strong and should stay as written — declaring that five AI-introduced errors were caught and corrected is exactly the right posture for an AI-open task and reads as diligence, not as a liability. Finally, a Q&A warning worth carrying into the prac: the single question I would ask this student is 'your main question is what the artefacts can and cannot tell a producer, but your only controlled comparison tests whether naming prefabs helps comprehension — how does that answer the main question?' Change 2 above is the fix, and having the answer ready is worth more than the edit.

marker_mitchell.persona: Mitchell McEwan, COMP3180 lecturer, marking with the CARS source-appraisal lens and a working-lecturer's test of whether an evaluation can actually be run week by week inside the stated hours and participant pool.

criteria.descriptor_quote: At least five distinct and high-quality sources with a common theme relating to the project topic. Sources are very well summarised and evaluated in terms of their relevance, lessons for and usefulness to the outlined project. Review synthesises and abstracts key patterns and relationships from the literature to motivate the project.
criteria.why_not_higher: Three things keep it off 'expertly summarised and insightfully evaluated'. (1) The appraisals are real but one clause deep, because the section is starved: the Literature Review runs 926 words against the template's 1,350 guide while the Project Proposal runs ~1,400 against ~900. On the criterion worth 45% that is a self-inflicted wound. (2) Currency, the CARS dimension I teach, is appraised for exactly one source ('Their evidence is narrow, four groups in one 1992 session, but the mechanism is incentives, not technology') and for none of the others. Ko et al. (2007) is field data on information needs predating Slack, modern trackers and AI summarisation, and the appraisal given — 'One company can skew how often a need arises but not what kinds exist, so I take the taxonomy, not the base rates' — is about generalisability, not age; Bertram et al. (2010) gets no currency note at all while its finding (bugs go unfiled) is 16 years old and tracker UIs have moved. (3) An entire evidence base is dismissed in one unappraised sentence: 'Washburn et al. (2016) sorted 155 game postmortems into 22 categories, none of them communication; postmortems cannot settle the question, so I look in artefacts.' No design, no sample limitation, no bias note — and it is carrying the weight of 'so I look in artefacts', which is the pivot of the whole proposal. Separately, 'Before that check, 86 of 119 rejected alerts had fired despite recent activity' is a number I cannot trace: 'rejected' by whom, and 'before that check' before what deployment change?
criteria.single_change_to_next_band: Move ~150 words out of Scoping Evidence and the Deliverables table into the Literature Review, and spend them on (a) a real appraisal of Washburn (design, coding scheme, why the absence of a communication category is weak evidence rather than no evidence) and (b) an explicit currency defence for Ko and Bertram. The section is 420 words under its own guide; it has the room the moment you stop paying for it elsewhere.

criteria.descriptor_quote: Outlines a sensible plan with clear and specific learning goals for developing industry-relevant skills. Identifies a considered research question with an appropriate and achievable mixed methodology for evaluation. Overview of scoping work undertaken provides a strongly convincing argument for the feasibility of the project. Includes a description of specific and measurable project deliverables clearly demonstrating these goals and satisfying unit requirements.
criteria.why_not_higher: The scoping is the best thing in this document and is genuinely at the HD line — a running Unity 6.4 Editor package on real SS3D data (Figure 2), a scripted corpus screen across six repositories (Figure 1), naming presence measured over nine weeks, a BuildReport probe and draft instruments (Appendices A–C). That is far past a hello-world. What stops me writing 'strongly convincing' across the whole feasibility argument is that the one input I cannot substitute for is the one with no evidence behind it. Everything mechanical is measured; the participant pool is asserted: 'I recruit at the Weeks 9 and 10 COMP3151 pracs and my COMP3180 prac' — no cohort size, no number of producers, no expression of interest — and the proposal itself names this as 'The biggest risk'. Three measurement statements also need a second reading before I know what would count as success. 'Sub-question 1 operationalises the main question' is scaffolding, not a question, so I have to reconstruct SQ1 from the sentence after it while SQ2 is written out properly. Deliverable 2's measure, '60% of changed prefabs and scenes named across the two study weeks', does not say whether 60% is a property of the corpus or the extractor's recall — and since Scoping Evidence says the study weeks were 'chosen from the three multi-commit weeks above 85%', on the first reading the measure cannot fail. And 'a fidelity check scores every claim in both weeks' reports against the team's record' never names the record: for SS3D the report is generated from the git history, so as written the check is checking the output against its own input. Two of four learning-goal measures ('I can state each mechanism unaided', 'I can tie each layout decision to a named reader need') are verifiable only by you.
criteria.single_change_to_next_band: Evidence the recruitment the way you evidenced the corpus: state the number of COMP3151 teams running in Weeks 9–10 and that each fields a producer, so the eight readers and the floor of five sit on a counted pool rather than an intention. Pay for it by cutting 'Sub-question 1 operationalises the main question.' and 'The prototype classifies files only.'

criteria.descriptor_quote: The report is easy to read and uses appropriate language and structure. It meets the word count, referencing and other submission requirements. It may contain a few minor spelling, grammatical or referencing errors.
criteria.why_not_higher: Referencing is the strongest part of this criterion: nineteen references, consistent APA, every one cited in the text and no orphans; three relevant, captioned, self-generated figures; word count met; template structure followed. I found no spelling or grammatical errors, which is above the CR descriptor. What blocks 'very easy to read' is density, and it is the same fault the A1 feedback named. The Study design paragraph is roughly 160 words carrying the design, the definition of Sub-question 1, the marking scheme, the eight-reader classification task, the agreement statistics and Sub-question 2 with no paragraph break to orient on. The Maddila paragraph ends on a 42-word sentence with an appositive that reads as a verb on first pass: 'Its limits set the bar for my challenge tier, flagging work gone quiet: every signal comes from inside one pull request and no verdict is composed across items, so mine must compose across items and read asset activity, or it adds nothing.' The Introduction opens plainly and well — 'Each week a game producer needs to know what changed' — and then its final paragraph front-loads study mechanics before the reader has the shape of the study: 'Two arms answer it. Eight readers sort ten common producer needs by which artefact could answer each.' Deliverable 1's success-measure cell is a 55-word run-on inside a table cell, in exactly the place a marker skims. I am reading a stack of these; several sentences here cost me a second pass.
criteria.single_change_to_next_band: Break the Study design paragraph in two at Sub-question 1 and write SQ1 out as a labelled question in the same form as SQ2. Costs no words, removes the densest block in the document, and is the single highest-leverage readability edit available.

top_changes.location: Literature Review — "Washburn et al. (2016) sorted 155 game postmortems into 22 categories, none of them communication; postmortems cannot settle the question, so I look in artefacts."
top_changes.problem: The 45% criterion is the one you have starved. The Literature Review is 926 words against a 1,350-word guide; the Project Proposal is ~1,400 against ~900. The symptom is visible here: an entire evidence base is dismissed in one sentence with no appraisal of design, coding scheme or bias, and that sentence is carrying the pivot of the proposal ('so I look in artefacts'). An absence of a category in someone else's coding scheme is weak evidence, not no evidence, and saying so is exactly the evaluative move the band above rewards.
top_changes.fix: Rebalance roughly 150 words from Project Proposal into Literature Review and spend the first ~50 here: "Washburn et al. (2016) coded 155 postmortems written by the teams themselves, into 22 inductive categories; none is communication. Self-authored retrospectives report what a team will admit in public, so the absence is evidence about postmortems, not about production. That is why I look in artefacts instead." Pay for it in Scoping Evidence: replace "Across nine sampled SS3D weeks, 16% to 100% of changed prefabs and scenes carry an object name in their changed text. Six clear the 60% naming target (Deliverable 2), so the two study weeks and a reserve come from those (Appendix A)." with "Six of nine sampled SS3D weeks clear the 60% naming target; the two study weeks and a reserve come from those (Appendix A)." (−25 words), and replace "No public Unity repository I screened links issues densely enough, nor does my own team's, where none of 126 commits cites a Jira issue (Appendix A)." with "No repository I screened links issues densely enough, including my own team's (Appendix A)." (−13 words). Both details survive in full in Appendix A.
top_changes.mark_impact: Literature Review +2 to +3; it is the only change here that moves the heaviest criterion, and it is word-neutral across the body.

top_changes.location: Scoping Evidence — "I recruit at the Weeks 9 and 10 COMP3151 pracs and my COMP3180 prac; proxies get a one-page scenario and stand in for studio producers, a limit I report."
top_changes.problem: This is the only feasibility claim in the document with nothing behind it, and the document itself calls recruitment 'The biggest risk'. You measured the corpus, the naming rates, the build report and the job ads and put all four in appendices; the eight readers rest on an intention. A marker who is asked to believe a plan runs week by week wants the pool counted the same way everything else is counted.
top_changes.fix: "COMP3151 runs [N] project teams this session, each with a producer; I recruit at its Weeks 9 and 10 pracs and my COMP3180 prac; proxies get a one-page scenario and stand in for studio producers, a limit I report." (+8 words). Pay for it by deleting "Sub-question 1 operationalises the main question." (−7, and change 3 removes it anyway) and "The prototype classifies files only." (−5, restated by the next sentence). If a cohort number is not available, name what is: how many producers you have already spoken to.
top_changes.mark_impact: Project Proposal +1 to +2 — it converts the feasibility argument from 'strongly convincing everywhere except participants' to strongly convincing.

top_changes.location: Scoping Evidence — "Sub-question 1 operationalises the main question. For each need surfaced by the tool study (Deliverable 1), which artefact could supply it, fully or partly: the tracker, the repository or the Unity asset layer? Each need is marked derivable, partly derivable or not."
top_changes.problem: Two faults in one place. Sub-question 2 is written out as a labelled question; Sub-question 1 is a sentence of scaffolding followed by an unlabelled question, so I have to reconstruct which sentence is the sub-question. And 'Each need is marked' is agentless — I only learn that you are the marker three clauses later, at 'against my marking'. Both sit inside a ~160-word paragraph that also carries the design, the eight-reader task, the agreement statistics and SQ2 with no break.
top_changes.fix: Start a new paragraph at this point and write: "Sub-question 1: for each need the tool study surfaces (Deliverable 1), which artefact could supply it, fully or partly — the tracker, the repository or the Unity asset layer? I mark each need derivable, partly derivable or not." Net −3 words and one new paragraph break.
top_changes.mark_impact: Communication +2 (the single biggest readability gain in the document); Project Proposal +1 for a research question a marker can find without reassembling it.

top_changes.location: Deliverables, row 2 — "60% of changed prefabs and scenes named across the two study weeks"
top_changes.problem: Ambiguous between a property of the corpus (how many files carry a name) and a property of the tool (how many the extractor resolves). On the first reading it is the corpus — and Scoping Evidence says the study weeks were 'chosen from the three multi-commit weeks above 85%', so the measure cannot fail. A success measure that is guaranteed by your own sampling is not a success measure. The target itself is fine; what it is measuring is not stated.
top_changes.fix: Word-neutral rewrite, keeping the 60%: "the extractor names 60% of the changed prefabs and scenes that carry a name, across the two study weeks". This makes it an extraction-recall target the tool can miss, which is what you actually want to evidence at A3.
top_changes.mark_impact: Project Proposal +1 — this is the one deliverable a strict marker would call unfalsifiable, and it is the Create goal's deliverable.

top_changes.location: Scoping Evidence — "Before any session, a fidelity check scores every claim in both weeks' reports against the team's record."
top_changes.problem: 'The team's record' is never named. For SS3D the report is generated from the git history, so on the plain reading the check scores the output against its own input and cannot fail. Given that you already identify hand-authored ground truth as a risk ('commit messages name the ticket, not the work'), the independent source needs naming in the sentence that claims the check.
top_changes.fix: "Before any session, a fidelity check scores every claim in both weeks' reports against each commit's diff and pull-request text, read by hand." (+3 words). Pay for it in the risks paragraph: "so an unscorable week is replaced and a contradicted claim repaired" → "so an unscorable week is replaced" (−5).
top_changes.mark_impact: Project Proposal +1 — makes the one internal-validity control in the study actually a control.

top_changes.location: Literature Review — "Before that check, 86 of 119 rejected alerts had fired despite recent activity."
top_changes.problem: I cannot trace this number, and it is load-bearing: it is the evidence that gates your challenge tier. 'Rejected' by whom — developers dismissing a notification, or the authors' own precision analysis? 'Before that check' — before which version of the deployment? A number whose referent is undefined is the first thing I check and the first thing I discount.
top_changes.fix: Name the agent and the stage, e.g. "Of 119 nudges developers dismissed as unwanted in the first deployment, 86 had fired on pull requests with activity in the previous day — which is why the 24-hour check exists." Pay for it by cutting "the lesson is how it avoids false alarms" (−8), which the rest of the paragraph states anyway. Verify the exact meaning of 'rejected' in Maddila et al. before rewording.
top_changes.mark_impact: Literature Review +1 — CARS Support: attributed statistics with a named referent.

top_changes.location: Learning Goals — "*Measure:* I can state each mechanism unaided, with its source and a breakdown it predicts." and "*Measure:* given an unfamiliar Unity week, I can tie each layout decision to a named reader need, two defended against a rejected alternative."
top_changes.problem: Two of your four measures can only be checked by the person claiming them. The other two are artefact-backed ('four tools coded'; 'every need classified against a named artefact') and are much stronger for it. At A3 a marker will have nothing to look at for Understand and Create, and the reflection is graded goal-by-goal against these.
top_changes.fix: Point both at an artefact you are already producing (Deliverable 8 is a weekly diary): "*Measure:* a diary entry stating each mechanism unaided, with its source and a breakdown it predicts." and "*Measure:* a diary entry tying each layout decision to a named reader need, two defended against a rejected alternative, written against an unfamiliar Unity week." Both are word-neutral.
top_changes.mark_impact: Project Proposal +1, and it protects the A3 Reflection criterion (15%) where the same goals are re-marked.

top_changes.location: Scoping Evidence — "proxies get a one-page scenario and stand in for studio producers, a limit I report."
top_changes.problem: You name the role proxy but not the project proxy. Your readers have never worked on SS3D, so a comprehension score measures cold reading of an unfamiliar repository, not a producer's awareness of their own week. That is arguably a harder test than the real one — which is a defensible argument, and one you do not make, so I have to raise it as an objection instead of reading it as a design choice.
top_changes.fix: "proxies get a one-page scenario and stand in for studio producers on a week none has worked on — a harder read than their own project, and a limit I report." (+6 words). Pay for it in the same section: "A pilot runs first; its data are excluded." → "A pilot runs first, excluded." (−4) and "in the follow-up" (−3).
top_changes.mark_impact: Project Proposal +0.5 to +1 — turns an unaddressed validity threat into a stated design position.

top_changes.location: Introduction — "Seven existing tools each cover one part of this (Appendix A)"
top_changes.problem: Appendix A's seventh row is McShaffry's 2013 GDC talk, which that same table describes as 'Manual; never productised' — not an existing tool. Your appendix header is honest ('Tool or source'); the body sentence is not. A number that does not survive a look at its own appendix is the cheapest thing for a marker to catch and the cheapest for you to fix.
top_changes.fix: Word-neutral: "Seven existing approaches each cover one part of this (Appendix A)". Apply the same wording wherever the count recurs.
top_changes.mark_impact: Communication +0.5 — small, but it is free and it is on page 1, where I form my first judgement about whether your numbers are traceable.

top_changes.location: Scoping Evidence — "Each session runs 45 minutes: 5 to brief, 12 per report to read it and answer six items (Appendix B), 6 for the ten-need sheet and 10 for the think-aloud and follow-up (six readers)."
top_changes.problem: 5 + 24 + 6 + 10 = 45 exactly. There is no slack for setup, for the verbal consent the next paragraph requires, or for a reader who is slower than planned — and a session that fits to the minute reads as arithmetic rather than a timing you expect to hold. It is the one place where the plan does not look like it has been run.
top_changes.fix: "Each session is booked for 50 minutes and runs to 45: 5 to brief, ..." (+3 words), and add consent to the brief. Pay for it with "eight readers show direction and failure points, not significance" → "n = 8 shows direction, not significance" (−5) in the quantitative-arm sentence.
top_changes.mark_impact: Project Proposal +0.5 — small, but this persona reads it as the difference between a plan and a schedule.

evidence_needed.item: What 'rejected alerts' means in Maddila et al. (2023), and which deployment stage 'before that check' refers to.
evidence_needed.what_would_settle_it: The paragraph in the Nudge paper reporting the 119/86 split, quoted in the verification file, with the paper's own word for who rejected the alerts.

evidence_needed.item: Whether Pascarella et al.'s 80%/30% is a share of repository files or a share of changed files, since Figure 1 measures changed-file entries and sits directly under that claim.
evidence_needed.what_would_settle_it: The methodology section of Pascarella et al. (2018). If the units differ, one clause — 'entries, not files, so the two are indicative rather than comparable' — belongs in the Figure 1 caption, which has the room.

evidence_needed.item: The number of COMP3151 teams running in Weeks 9–10 and how many field a producer.
evidence_needed.what_would_settle_it: The COMP3151 team list or iLearn group count; or, better, two or three named expressions of interest already secured.

evidence_needed.item: Which of the six counted sources have been read in full (the bracketed line after the GenAI statement).
evidence_needed.what_would_settle_it: A potted summary of each in your own words, written before the proposal goes in. Every source you cite can come up in a prac conversation, and a source you cannot restate unaided reads differently in person than on the page.

evidence_needed.item: Whether Deliverable 2's 60% is an extraction-recall target or a corpus property.
evidence_needed.what_would_settle_it: A run of the committed-tier extractor over one already-measured week, reporting names resolved over names present. That number is also the honest baseline for the A3 result.

marker_mitchell.notes: Honest expectation for the real mark: low-to-mid 70s, call it 72–77, with the risk skewed down rather than up. The scoping evidence is what protects this proposal — a working Editor package on real data, a scripted corpus screen, nine measured weeks, a build probe and draft instruments is more than I usually see at A2, and it is the reason I am marking D and not CR on the Project Proposal. The thing that will cost marks is the same thing that cost them at A1: compression. This document is more disciplined than that presentation and it opens with a plain sentence a non-specialist can follow, which is real progress; but several sentences still carry three ideas and need a second pass, and the Study design paragraph is the worst offender. If only one change is made from this list, make number 3 — it costs nothing and removes the densest block. If two, add number 1: the criterion worth 45% is 420 words under its own guide while the 40% criterion runs 500 over, and that is a straight reallocation, not new writing. Mechanical notes, none of which I have priced into the marks: the bracketed '[CONFIRM BEFORE SUBMISSION…]' line must go, and I have marked as though it already had; there is no table-of-contents field, which I have accepted; page 1 carries the same running string as both header and footer, which is cosmetic but looks unconsidered; the reference list is clean — nineteen entries, consistent APA, every one cited, no orphans — and Nielsen (1994) appears only inside the Deliverables table, which is legitimate but worth knowing. Word count is met at 2,470 body plus a 26-word cover. One last observation on engagement, since I said in class that weekly prac presence is what evidences A3: this plan is built to run in pracs — recruitment at the Weeks 9 and 10 COMP3151 pracs, the pilot in Week 11, sessions in Weeks 11 and 12 — which is exactly the right shape. Make sure the diary in Deliverable 8 starts now rather than in Week 9, because the engagement criterion reads the whole session, not the back half.
